grammar_points.name: 〜ている (te iru) — progressive / ongoing state

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb て-form (te-form) + いる (iru) expresses either (1) an ongoing action — "is doing ~," or (2) a resulting state — "has done ~ (and the result remains)." In casual speech, いる (iru) contracts to る (ru): 食べている (tabete iru) → 食べてる (tabeteru). This is one of the most essential patterns in Japanese.

Example from this song:
いつも笑っている (itsumo waratte iru) — "is always smiling"
Describes a habitual, ongoing state — someone who constantly smiles.

More examples:
• 今、本を読んでいる (ima, hon o yonde iru) — "I'm reading a book right now" (ongoing action)
• 窓が開いている (mado ga aite iru) — "the window is open" (resulting state)
• もう食べてる (mou tabeteru) — "already eating" (casual contraction)

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 笑う (warau, "to smile/laugh") → 笑って (waratte, te-form) → 笑っている (waratte iru, "is smiling")

grammar_points.name: 〜てみせる (te miseru) — I'll show you I can!

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb て-form (te-form) + みせる (miseru, "to show") expresses strong determination — "I will definitely do ~ (and prove it)!" or "I'll show you that I can ~!" It is a declaration of resolve. Literally, it means "I will do ~ and show (the result)." This is a powerful, confident expression.

Example from this song:
The singer declares with conviction that they will achieve something and prove it to the world.

More examples:
• 絶対に勝ってみせる (zettai ni katte miseru) — "I will win, I'll show you!"
• 夢を叶えてみせる (yume o kanaete miseru) — "I will make my dream come true, just watch!"
• 最後まで生き延びてみせる (saigo made ikinobite miseru) — "I'll survive to the end, I promise!"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: Verb て-form (te-form) + みせる (miseru, "to show") → "I'll prove I can ~!"

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb て-form (te-form) + も (mo) means "even if ~" or "even though ~." It states that the result will not change regardless of the condition. For い-adjectives (i-adjectives): drop い (i), add くても (kutemo). For な-adjectives (na-adjectives)/nouns: add でも (demo). This is fundamental for expressing resilience and determination.

Example from this song:
Used to express that obstacles will not stop the singer — even if they fall, they will get back up.

More examples:
• 雨が降っても行く (ame ga futte mo iku) — "even if it rains, I'll go"
• どんなに辛くても (donna ni tsurakutemo) — "no matter how painful"
• 失敗しても諦めない (shippai shitemo akiramenai) — "even if I fail, I won't give up"

grammar_points.name: 〜続ける (tsuzukeru) — to continue doing

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb ます-stem (masu-stem) + 続ける (tsuzukeru) means "to continue doing ~" or "to keep doing ~." It emphasizes that an action persists without stopping. 続ける (tsuzukeru) conjugates as a normal ichidan verb: 続けた (tsuzuketa, past), 続けている (tsuzukete iru, is continuing).

Example from this song:
The song emphasizes persistent action — continuing to run, continuing to believe, never stopping.

More examples:
• 書き続ける (kaki tsuzukeru) — "keep writing"
• 待ち続けた (machi tsuzuketa) — "kept waiting"
• 歩き続けよう (aruki tsuzukeyou) — "let's keep walking"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: Verb ます-stem (masu-stem) + 続ける (tsuzukeru, "to continue") → "keep doing ~"

grammar_points.name: 〜んだろう (n darou) — I wonder / it must be that

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb/Adjective plain form + んだろう (n darou) combines the explanatory の/ん (no/n, "the fact is") with だろう (darou, "probably / I wonder"). It can express (1) wondering — "I wonder if ~" or (2) conjecture — "it must be that ~." It is softer than a direct question and is common in internal monologue and song lyrics.

Example from this song:
The singer wonders about their path — reflecting on what they should do or what might happen.

More examples:
• どうしてだろう (doushite darou) — "I wonder why"
• 幸せなんだろうか (shiawase nan darou ka) — "I wonder if I'm happy"
• きっと大丈夫なんだろう (kitto daijoubu nan darou) — "it must be okay, surely"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: Verb/Adjective plain form + ん (n) + だろう (darou) → "I wonder if ~" / "it must be ~"

grammar_points.name: 〜ず (zu) — without doing (literary negative)

explanation.en:
How it works:
The ending 〜ず (zu) is the classical Japanese negative form, equivalent to modern ないで (naide, "without doing"). To form it: take the ない-form stem and add ず (zu). For する (suru), it becomes せず (sezu). For example: 食べない (tabenai) → 食べず (tabezu). It sounds more literary and formal, making it common in songs and written Japanese.

Example from this song:
The singer describes doing something "without" another action — pressing forward without hesitation, without looking back.

More examples:
• 何も言わず去った (nani mo iwazu satta) — "left without saying anything"
• 休まず働いた (yasumazu hataraita) — "worked without resting"
• 諦めずに頑張る (akiramezu ni ganbaru) — "persevere without giving up"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: Verb ない-form stem + ず (zu) → "without doing ~"
